stemMd: A freight crate is loaded with $p$ boxes of type P, which weigh $18$ kilograms each, and $q$ boxes of type Q, which weigh $30$ kilograms each, and nothing else. The total weight of the boxes can be at most $480$ kilograms, and the crate must contain at least twice as many type P boxes as type Q boxes. What is the greatest possible value of $q$?
explanationMd:
Translate each condition into an inequality, then ask what the second condition costs you when you try to make $q$ large.

- Weight: $18p + 30q \le 480$
- "At least twice as many P boxes as Q boxes": the number of P boxes is at least $2$ times the number of Q boxes, so $p \ge 2q$.

To fit as many Q boxes as possible, use as few P boxes as the rule allows, which is $p = 2q$ (any extra P box only adds weight). Substitute into the weight condition:

$$18(2q) + 30q \le 480$$
$$66q \le 480$$
$$q \le \frac{480}{66} \approx 7.27$$

The number of boxes must be a whole number, so the greatest possible value is $q = 7$.

Check that $7$ is actually achievable and $8$ is not. With $q = 7$ and $p = 14$: $18(14) + 30(7) = 252 + 210 = 462 \le 480$, and $14 \ge 2(7)$. With $q = 8$ the crate needs $p \ge 16$, and even $p = 16$ gives $288 + 240 = 528 > 480$.

The translation step is the one to slow down on. "At least twice as many P as Q" puts the $2$ next to $q$, not next to $p$: test it with numbers, since $10$ P boxes and $5$ Q boxes should satisfy it, and $10 \ge 2(5)$ does.

distractorRationale.b: This rounds $\frac{480}{66} \approx 7.27$ up to the nearest whole number. The bound is a maximum, so rounding up breaks it: $8$ Q boxes need at least $16$ P boxes, and together they weigh $528$ kilograms.
distractorRationale.c: This writes the ratio condition backwards as $2p \ge q$. Then the fewest P boxes allowed is $\frac{q}{2}$, the weight condition becomes $9q + 30q = 39q \le 480$, and $q \le 12.3$, giving $12$. That inequality says the Q boxes may number up to twice the P boxes, which is a different rule.
distractorRationale.d: This uses only the weight limit, $30q \le 480$, as if the crate could hold Q boxes alone. It ignores the requirement that there be at least twice as many P boxes, which forces extra weight onto every Q box.

accessibilityText: A crate holds p boxes of type P at 18 kilograms each and q boxes of type Q at 30 kilograms each. Total weight is at most 480 kilograms, and there must be at least twice as many type P boxes as type Q boxes. Find the greatest possible q. The four choices are 7, 8, 12 and 16.

provenance.notes: Original item. Weights chosen so the correct combined coefficient (66) and the reversed-translation coefficient (39) give different whole-number caps, and so that the unrounded bound invites rounding up.

review.author: wave7-sat-math-alg-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Weight is lowest when p = 2q, giving 36q + 30q = 66q <= 480, so q <= 7.27. Box counts are whole numbers, so q = 7 (with p = 14, the weight is 462). For q = 8, p must be at least 16, giving 528 > 480. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-sat-math-run1) reached the same answer: To make q as large as possible, take p as small as allowed, p = 2q. Then 36q + 30q = 66q <= 480, so q <= 7.27. Checking integers: q = 7 with p = 14 weighs 462 kg, which works. q = 8 forces p >= 16, and 288 + 240 = 528 > 480, which fails. So the greatest q is 7.]

review.notes: Author solved twice and checked by brute force over whole-number p and q: the greatest q satisfying 18p + 30q <= 480 and p >= 2q is 7 (with p = 14); the reversed rule 2p >= q gives 12, the weight limit alone gives 16, and rounding 480/66 up gives 8. Hard: two constraints must be combined by choosing the binding case, the verbal ratio must be translated in the right direction, and the integer cap must be taken downward. Awaiting a blind independent solve before publication.
